item.title: Sound
item.description:
A container can play sound in the playground. It is opt-in, like the GPU:

$ wctr run -d --audio tone # a 440 Hz sine; click the page once
$ wctr run --rm --gpu --audio -m 512m quake --map e1m1

Engine v0.40.0 adds run --audio (the device capability audio, independent of --gpu, with no option) and the host module wctr_audio_out. It is not a wasi_ module: no WASI proposal covers audio (the proposal list has no audio, PCM or media entry in any phase), so the import is private, like wasi_webgpu_batch, and is kept small so that it can be lowered onto a standard one if one appears. The design, with its prior art and threat model, is docs/audio-design.md in the engine.

What a guest sees

Four core-wasm functions, every parameter an i32, every result an errno. Output only: there is no capture.

Function Effect
stream_open(rate, channels, capacity, out) rate 8000 to 48000 Hz, 1 or 2 channels, capacity 256 to 16384 frames (a power of two). The handle is stored at out. The host never picks another rate: out of bounds is InvalidArgument
stream_write(stream, ptr, frames, out) copies and queues up to frames interleaved little-endian float32 frames, never blocking; stores {accepted, queued}. frames = 0 is a poll. Samples are clamped to [-1, 1] and a non-finite one becomes 0
stream_stats(stream, out) stores {played, underruns, refused, state}; state is 0 waiting, 1 playing, 2 closed
stream_close(stream) closes it; the process ending does too

Errors: Denied (no --audio), Unsupported (no audio provider: native wctr has no audio output), TooLarge, QuotaExceeded (2 streams per container, 8 per page), Fault (a range outside the guest’s memory, computed in 64 bits).

The page

The engine worker allocates one SharedArrayBuffer ring per stream and the page plays it through an AudioWorklet (the audioring module of wasmbox, served as audio-worklet.js, byte for byte), one AudioContext for the page. A browser lets a page play sound only after a user gesture, so click the page once (or press a key in it). Until then the stream is waiting: the host accepts what the container writes and discards it, so sound made before the click is never played late. The host knows the page plays from a heartbeat the worklet advances every render quantum.

Volume and mute work at two levels. Each container’s dashboard pane (the Surfaces view, dashboard v0.12.0) has a sound line with Vol -, Vol + (steps of 10) and Mute for the sound of its container, and a Sound strip at the bottom left of the page has the page-wide mute all. They are gain nodes between the worklet and the speakers, so a container cannot undo them. A container with no surface has no pane, so no per-container control. The end-to-end test clicks the pane’s buttons against Quake’s real sound: what reaches the speakers over what the worklet played is 1.000 at full volume and 0.300 at 30 %, and 0 muted.

tone

wctr run -d --audio tone [--hz N] [--silent] [--seconds N] plays a sine (440 Hz, 11025 Hz stereo, amplitude 0.25), keeping 60 ms queued. It prints the mean cost of a stream_write call at the end (one engine round trip each; about 0.2 ms in headless Chromium on an Apple-silicon Mac). Without --audio it prints that the host answered denied and exits 2.

The end-to-end test (headless Chromium with --autoplay-policy=document-user-activation-required) asserts the context is suspended before any gesture, clicks, and over 2 s asserts that at least half of the frames played, the analyser’s peak is in the 440 Hz bin (plus or minus one), the RMS is above -30 dBFS and fewer than 5 underruns happened. Four planted negatives must each fail their own assertion: tone --silent (the RMS), tone --hz 880 (the frequency), no click (nothing plays, the context stays suspended) and no --audio (denied, no stream).

Quake with sound

The quake image does not run with --audio by default; add it (wctr run --rm --gpu --audio -m 512m quake). The game’s backend opens one stream (11025 Hz stereo, 1024 frames), converts its mix to float32 and writes once a tic; the host’s answer is the queue its mixer is paced by. Without the grant, on native wctr, or in a build without the wctraudio tag, the game plays silent and raises nothing.

The mixer used to paint a fixed 512 frames a tic, whatever the tic’s length: 2.8 times real time at 60 tics a second. It is now paced like tyrquake’s S_Update (go-quake1/engine v0.22.0). Measured as mix frames offered per second of game time over the 11025 an output plays, in headless Chromium on a real GPU (300 frames of e1m1): 2.77 before, 1.01 after.

The mixer runs in the page’s worklet

With go-quake1/engine v0.56.0 and go-wasmcontainers/engine v0.49.0 the game no longer mixes on its own thread. It loads its samples once and sends play, stop and volume commands (the voices of wctr_audio_out); the page’s AudioWorklet (wasmbox audioring v0.3.0, the wasmbox-voices worklet) paints the voices 0.1 s ahead on the audio thread. A garbage collection or a slow frame on the game’s thread then cannot starve the speakers: the game prints QUAKE: sound on (wctr_audio_out voices, mixed in the page), and --fixed-mixer forces the old single stream.

How a guest and its GPU host worker attach

A guest’s GPU calls are served by a second worker (role=host), so a present or a submit does not wait for the engine’s thread. Since go-wasmcontainers/engine v0.49.1 the guest’s memory (a SharedArrayBuffer) and the control block do not travel on the guest’s own port: the guest posts its memory to the engine, the engine relays it on its control channel to the host worker as {t: "attach"}, and the host answers {t: "attached"} on the guest’s port. The guest starts only after that answer (or traps with “the gpu host worker did not answer” after 30 s). Firefox keeps a message body that carries a SharedArrayBuffer in a table keyed by the sending port and forgets it when that port closes, so the old way ended in attach-refused there (go-wasmcontainers/engine#84).
